classydms — project context for Claude / future contributors

Source: CLAUDE.md

This file gives context for AI assistants and future contributors picking up this codebase. For end-user documentation, see the pkgdown site at https://mljaniczek.github.io/classydms and README.md.

What this package does

classydms is an R package implementing an end-to-end pipeline for disease vs control classification from Gas Chromatography Differential Mobility Spectrometry (GC-DMS) data. Each subject’s GC-DMS spectrum is a 2-D image of ion intensity over retention time (RT) and compensation voltage (CV). Peaks in this image correspond to volatile organic compounds (VOCs); the hypothesis is that disease alters the VOC signature in a way that can be detected by a classifier and used to nominate candidate biomarker compounds.

The fundamental challenge is small clinical sample sizes (~100-200 subjects per disease) combined with large per-sample data (~10^5 pixels of structured signal). Conventional deep learning approaches overfit catastrophically at this n/p ratio.

The package’s answer is self-supervised pretraining on synthetic data: estimate the peak parameter distributions from real samples (label-agnostic), generate millions of parametric synthetic GC-DMS images matching those distributions, train a ResNet-style encoder on a denoising autoencoder task with those synthetic images, then transfer the frozen encoder to a tiny elastic net classifier on the 64-dim global-average-pooled features. The elastic net coefficients identify which encoder channels are predictive; weighted spatial activations produce a saliency map in (RT, CV) coordinates that can be cross-referenced with compound libraries to nominate biomarker candidates.

Pipeline at a glance

raw .xls -> read_dms_file -> load_dms_directory  (returns samples + y)
       -> process_one_sample (SG + AsLS)
       -> baseline_basement (dust threshold)
       -> trim_bounds_from_occupancy + pooled_trim_bounds + trim_sample
       -> normalize_sample (log + quantile)
       -> pad_to_target (multiple of 32 for stride compatibility)
   ===
       -> estimate_peak_params (label-agnostic)
       -> generate_one_synthetic / generate_synthetic_dataset
       -> pretrain_denoising_online (writes encoder.pt + autoencoder.pt + manifest)
   ===
       -> cv_encoder_elastic_net          (interpretable classifier)
       -> extract_encoder_features        (or feed to your own classifier)
       -> aggregate_saliency_masked       (CAM via elastic net coefs)
       -> map hotspots to (RT, CV) -> compound libraries

Key design decisions, with rationale

Preprocessing

  • Savitzky-Golay smoothing along RT only (not CV): RT has dense sampling (~1500 points), CV has ~50 voltage steps. Smoothing across CV would merge adjacent peaks.
  • AsLS baseline correction (Eilers & Boelens 2005), not polynomial or rolling-ball: it handles the wide range of peak widths simultaneously present.
  • Per-sample relative dust threshold = 1% of Q_0.95 of positive pixels: robust to inter-sample / inter-instrument intensity differences that a fixed global threshold would mishandle.
  • Pre-thresholded matrix retained as sample$Z_pretrim for accurate peak-width estimation later: dust thresholding zeros out peak flanks, which would bias FWHM measurements narrow.
  • Cohort-wide trim bounds via robust quantiles (q_lo=0.05, q_hi=0.95): one outlier sample doesn’t force the cohort to lose content nearly all others have.
  • Padding to multiple of 32: matches total RT downsampling factor through the encoder (4 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32), so spatial dims work out cleanly.
  • Center placement when padding (not top-left): convolutional filters encounter zero-padding equally on all sides.

Synthetic generation

  • Label-agnostic: peak distributions are pooled across all samples regardless of class. This is the safeguard against information leakage from the synthetic pretraining stage into downstream classification.
  • Log-normal fits for sigma and intensity: right-skewed, positive-only quantities that empirically match the data.
  • norm_clamp = 10 safety bound on normalized synthetic pixels: rare sparse synthetic images can have near-zero Q_0.95 after log-transform, which would blow up the normalization denominator. The clamp keeps such outliers from destabilizing training.
  • size_jitter = 0.6 per-peak log-normal scale factor: adds size diversity beyond what the fitted sigma distributions alone provide. Exposed as a function parameter (default 0.6).

Pretraining

  • Online generation via pretrain_denoising_online: memory cost is constant (one batch at a time) regardless of total samples seen. Lets the model see hundreds of thousands to millions of unique synthetic samples on a laptop. The batch trainer (pretrain_autoencoder) is kept for small-scale experiments and as a clearer reference implementation.
  • Gradient clipping at L2 norm 1.0: prevents outlier batches from destabilizing optimization.
  • Fixed validation set (val_n = 200 by default) held constant across epochs: gives a stable progress metric the otherwise-random online training loss can’t provide.
  • Every-epoch save of encoder + autoencoder + manifest: ensures a mid-run crash always leaves recoverable artifacts.
  • Periodic numbered checkpoints (checkpoint_every): roll back to a specific earlier epoch if needed.
  • resume_from parameter: pick up training from an interrupted run, inheriting prior loss history. Caveat: Adam moments are NOT restored.

Classification

  • Encoder feature extraction (GAP) → elastic net is the recommended path, not a neural network classifier head. With 64 features and ~200 samples, regularized logistic regression is well-conditioned, interpretable, and stable. The NN head path (cv_pretrained_oof) is retained for comparison but has been less reliable in practice.
  • Deep-clone encoder per fold inside build_pretrained_classifier: R torch’s nn_module objects are reference-based. Without the deep clone, multiple CV folds share the same encoder state, and any unfreeze_last_block = TRUE fine-tuning leaks across fold boundaries (we observed AUCs of 0.99+ from this bug). encoder$clone(deep = TRUE) is non-negotiable here.

Interpretability

  • CAM via elastic net coefficients, not Grad-CAM: because the elastic net classifier head is linear in the GAP features, the saliency map S_i(h, w) = sum_c(beta_c * F_i^(c)(h, w)) is mathematically equivalent to CAM with elastic net coefs as head weights. No backprop required.
  • Masked aggregation across samples (aggregate_saliency_masked): the data/padding boundary creates artifact stripes if you naively average. Mask by each sample’s original (non-padded) dims and divide pixel-wise by the per-pixel count.

Critical lessons learned (read this if classifier AUCs look suspicious)

  1. Cross-fold encoder leakage — nn_module objects are reference-based. Multiple folds sharing the same encoder is a silent bug that can produce AUCs in the 0.95+ range that look real but are leakage. Fixed by encoder$clone(deep = TRUE) in build_pretrained_classifier.
  2. NA noise on aggressive dust thresholds — when basement_thr is larger than robust_eps, no pixels fall in the (0, eps] range, so the noise estimator collects no samples and returns NA. Synthetic generation then produces NaN tensors. Fixed by fallback to 0.1% of median peak intensity in estimate_peak_params, plus a belt-and-suspenders check in generate_one_synthetic.
  3. Sample-level metadata leakage — sample-level statistics (RT length, total signal, mean intensity) can themselves separate classes in some cohorts (e.g., acquisition-batch confounders). If AUC on encoder features is high but you can’t find spatial saliency, check the metadata first.
  4. Encoder mode collapse — on some runs, only a handful of the 64 encoder channels carry meaningful per-sample variance after GAP. Elastic net then inflates near-zero-variance “phantom” channels into apparent importance. Diagnose by inspecting feature variances: apply(elnet$features, 2, var). Mitigations: longer pretraining, larger size_jitter, more synthetic diversity.
  5. R session crashes during long pretrain runs on Apple Silicon — sometimes due to memory pressure or MPS issues. Mitigations: gc() between epochs, every-epoch save, resume_from for recovery.

Open questions / outstanding work

  • AKI vs Flu disparity — preliminary experiments showed Flu AUC ~0.78 vs AKI AUC ~0.48 with the same encoder. This may indicate Flu is exploiting a cohort-specific artifact rather than chemistry. Needs more disease settings to establish a baseline of what “real biology” looks like.
  • Grad-CAM as an alternative interpretability path — would be useful to compare to the CAM-via-elastic-net approach on the same encoder.
  • Two-channel (POS + NEG) fusion — currently only POS is used. Negative-channel information may be complementary.
  • Sensitivity analysis on preprocessing parameters — SG window, AsLS λ, dust threshold, trim occupancy thresholds. Currently all hand-tuned defaults; the existing sensitivity_analysis_peak_params framework could be extended.
  • Cross-disease pretraining — pretrain on a pooled multi-disease cohort instead of (or in addition to) parametric synthetic data.

Potential optimizations (not yet implemented)

Parallel synthetic data generation

The generate_one_synthetic loop inside pretrain_denoising_online’s generate_batch() is serial in R. On CPU runs this is ~30-40% of wall time. On MPS runs (where GPU forward/backward is fast) it becomes a larger relative fraction — possibly ~50% on M-series Pro/Max chips.

A fork-based parallelization via parallel::mclapply would give a ~2-4x speedup for the data-generation portion. Implementation: replace the for loop in generate_batch() with parallel::mclapply (Unix/ macOS only; Windows would need parallel::parLapply and a cluster). Need to be careful about RNG seeding so each fork produces independent samples — mc.set.seed = TRUE handles this.

Not implemented yet because: (a) on CPU the speedup is partial since torch already parallelizes the bigger chunk; (b) on MPS the run is already fast enough that wall-clock isn’t a blocker; (c) adds platform-specific complexity. Worth revisiting if scaling to >5M synthetic samples or if users on Windows need it.

Larger batch sizes on MPS

Default batch_size = 32. M-series GPUs (especially M4 Max with 40 GPU cores) can comfortably handle 64 or 128 with substantial throughput gain, because GPU kernel launch overhead amortizes better on bigger batches. Activity Monitor GPU utilization < 70% during training is a signal there’s headroom. Increase batch size, halve steps_per_epoch to keep total sample count constant.

Mixed precision

Could enable float16 (or bfloat16) on MPS for further speedup and memory savings. R torch supports torch_half() but the autoencoder hasn’t been tested in mixed precision. Numerical stability of the denoising MSE loss in fp16 is a concern — would need careful validation. Not currently a priority given MPS-fp32 is already fast.

Pre-allocated batch buffer

generate_batch() allocates fresh clean_arr and noisy_arr R arrays every call. For a million-sample run that’s 31k+ allocations. Reusing a pre-allocated buffer would shave a small fraction of wall time and reduce GC pressure. Marginal but easy.

pretrain_denoising_online() as pretrain_denoising_*()

The function is getting long. Could split out the manifest/checkpoint/save logic into a helper function and the training loop into another, making each component easier to test and modify. Not urgent.

Code conventions

  • roxygen2 for all exported functions with @param, @return, @export. Internal helpers get @keywords internal.
  • Namespaced calls (torch::torch_tensor) preferred over library() imports inside functions — easier to debug, more explicit.
  • Snake_case for function and parameter names.
  • No tidyverse in R/ — tidyverse packages are in Suggests for vignettes only. R/*.R uses base R + purrr (for map_dbl etc.).
  • globalVariables() in zzz.R to silence false-positive R CMD check notes about torch’s .. and self.
  • .Rbuildignore keeps sampledata/, *.pt, *.Rdata, _pkgdown.yml, docs/, .github/ out of the package tarball.

When testing changes

  • devtools::check() should report 0 errors, 0 warnings. The occasional “future file timestamps” NOTE is a CRAN-side issue and can be ignored.
  • tests/testthat/test_loader_smoke.R runs the full pipeline end-to-end against sampledata/ when invoked interactively from the package root. Use it to verify any change to the preprocessing / synthetic / pretrain path.
  • pkgdown::build_site(new_process = FALSE) rebuilds the site locally for preview before pushing.

Related repos / context

  • Research repo (private): mljaniczek/skin_voc_gcdms2 — this is where ad-hoc experiments and hyperparameter sweeps live. The package is the polished extraction of the stable subset.
  • The dissertation chapter built on this work is in mljaniczek/dissertation (or wherever Margaret’s dissertation repo lives).

Notes for future Claude sessions

  • The pipeline is end-to-end working on the influenza sample data as of the most recent commit. If something breaks, run tests/testthat/test_loader_smoke.R first to isolate which stage.
  • Always re-run devtools::document() after changing roxygen comments so man/*.Rd and NAMESPACE stay in sync. The pkgdown GitHub Action will fail check if they don’t.
  • MPS is the right device on Apple Silicon. Don’t try to “fix” the slow CPU runs — that’s just the wrong device.
  • The deep clone in build_pretrained_classifier is critical. Do not “optimize” it away.
  • The dust threshold / noise NA path in estimate_peak_params has caused crashes twice in development. Don’t simplify the fallback logic.
  • The Influenza vs AKI discrepancy is a known open question, not a bug. Future analyses on more disease cohorts will help resolve whether it’s biology or artifact.
